text: Bettino Ricasoli, 1st Count of Brolio, 2nd Baron Ricasoli (Italian pronunciation: [betˈtiːno riˈkaːzoli]; 9 March 1809 – 23 October 1880), was an Italian statesman who played a central role in Italy’s politics during and after the unification of Italy. He led the Moderate Party. Born in Florence, Ricasoli became an orphan at eighteen and, with his family estate heavily in debt, was declared of age by special decree of the Grand Duke of Tuscany and entrusted with the guardianship of his younger brothers. He was Catholic. After interrupting his studies, he moved to Brolio, where he carefully managed the family’s assets and disencumbered them. In 1847, he founded the journal La Patria and submitted a memorial to the Grand Duke proposing solutions to state difficulties. In 1848, he was elected Gonfaloniere of Florence but resigned due to the Grand Duke’s anti-Liberal policies. As Tuscan minister of the interior in 1859, he promoted the union of Tuscany with Piedmont, which occurred on March 12, 1860. Elected an Italian deputy in 1861, he succeeded Cavour as premier. In this role, he admitted Garibaldian volunteers to the regular army, revoked the exile decree against Mazzini, and sought reconciliation with the Vatican, though these efforts were blocked by the pope’s non possumus. Disdainful of his rival Rattazzi, he resigned in 1862 but returned to power in 1866. During this time, he refused Napoleon III’s offer to cede Venetia to Italy on the condition that Italy abandon the Prussian alliance, and also declined the Prussian decoration of the Black Eagle because La Marmora, the architect of the alliance, was not to receive it. After the French troops left Rome in late 1866, he attempted to reconcile with the Vatican through a convention in which Italy would return Church property from suppressed religious orders in exchange for a gradual payment of 24,000,000; to appease the Vatican, he granted exequatur to forty-five bishops opposed to the Italian regime. The Vatican accepted the proposal, but the Italian Chamber remained resistant, and although Ricasoli dissolved it, it returned more hostile than before. Without awaiting a vote, he resigned and withdrew from political life, speaking in the Chamber only rarely. He died at his Castello di Brolio on 23 October 1880. The barone developed the modern recipe of Chianti wine; although a specific formula with grape percentages is often incorrectly attributed to him, his shift to Sangiovese as the primary grape in the blend had lasting effects on Tuscan and Italian wine. The family-owned firm Ricasoli 1141 continues to produce wine at Brolio. His private life and public service were defined by integrity and strict austerity, earning him the title of the Iron Baron. Despite the failure of his ecclesiastical initiative, he remains one of the most significant figures of the Italian Risorgimento.
